claim: Active whisking is an important model sensorimotor behavior.
source: Active whisking is an important model sensorimotor behavior, but the function of the cerebellum in the rodent whisker system is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific consensus about the whisker system as a model.

claim: The function of the cerebellum in the rodent whisker system is unknown.
source: Active whisking is an important model sensorimotor behavior, but the function of the cerebellum in the rodent whisker system is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Purkinje cell spiking activity changes strongly during whisking bouts.
source: We show that Purkinje cell spiking activity changes strongly during whisking bouts.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental recordings from Purkinje cells during whisking behavior.

claim: On average, the changes in simple spike rate coincide with or slightly precede movement.
source: On average, the changes in simple spike rate coincide with or slightly precede movement, indicating that the synaptic drive responsible for these changes is predominantly of efferent (motor) rather than re-afferent (sensory) origin.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis of simple spike rates relative to whisker movement onset.

claim: The synaptic drive responsible for simple spike rate changes is predominantly of efferent (motor) rather than re-afferent (sensory) origin.
source: On average, the changes in simple spike rate coincide with or slightly precede movement, indicating that the synaptic drive responsible for these changes is predominantly of efferent (motor) rather than re-afferent (sensory) origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal relationship between neural activity and movement.

claim: On-going changes in simple spike rate provide an accurate linear read-out of whisker set point.
source: Remarkably, on-going changes in simple spike rate provide an accurate linear read-out of whisker set point.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between simple spike rates and whisker position.

claim: Purkinje cells integrate parallel fiber input to generate precise information about whisking kinematics through linear changes in firing rate.
source: Thus, despite receiving several hundred thousand discrete synaptic inputs across a non-linear dendritic tree, Purkinje cells integrate parallel fiber input to generate precise information about whisking kinematics through linear changes in firing rate.
evidence: This is based on the observed linear relationship between firing rate and whisker position, combined with knowledge of Purkinje cell anatomy.

claim: Purkinje cells receive several hundred thousand discrete synaptic inputs across a non-linear dendritic tree.
source: Thus, despite receiving several hundred thousand discrete synaptic inputs across a non-linear dendritic tree, Purkinje cells integrate parallel fiber input to generate precise information about whisking kinematics through linear changes in firing rate.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about Purkinje cells, supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Tactile sensation is an active process whereby sensory information is acquired through self-initiated movement.
source: Tactile sensation is an active process whereby sensory information is acquired through self-initiated movement.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific understanding about active sensing.

claim: Effective sensory processing involves the interplay between motor and sensory systems, incorporating multiple feedback loops.
source: Effective sensory processing therefore involves the interplay between motor and sensory systems, incorporating multiple feedback loops (Diamond et al., 2008; Matyas et al., 2010; Bosman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Rodents use coordinated whisker movements for tactile exploration and discrimination, rhythmically sweeping their whiskers back and forth to scan their surroundings.
source: Rodents use coordinated whisker movements for tactile exploration and discrimination, rhythmically sweeping their whiskers back and forth to scan their surroundings.
evidence: This is established knowledge about rodent whisking behavior.

claim: The rodent whisker system provides an attractive model to tackle questions related to active sensory processing and sensorimotor integration.
source: The rodent whisker system thus provides an attractive model to tackle questions related to active sensory processing (O'Connor et al., 2002; Crochet et al., 2011) and sensorimotor integration (Kleinfeld et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research using this model system.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is a major site of sensorimotor integration.
source: Amongst multiple processing regions in the brain, the cerebellar cortex is a major site of sensorimotor integration, but little is known about its role in active whisking.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar function.

claim: Little is known about the cerebellar cortex's role in active whisking.
source: Amongst multiple processing regions in the brain, the cerebellar cortex is a major site of sensorimotor integration, but little is known about its role in active whisking.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The lateral hemispheres of the cerebellum, in particular lobule Crus I, are strongly implicated in vibrissae sensorimotor loops.
source: The lateral hemispheres of the cerebellum, in particular lobule Crus I, are strongly implicated in these vibrissae sensorimotor loops (Shambes et al., 1978; Bosman et al., 2011; Proville et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Synchronization of activity occurs between the cerebellum and other whisker-related brain regions both under anesthesia and during active whisking in the awake state.
source: Growing evidence suggests synchronization of activity between the cerebellum and other whisker-related brain regions both under anesthesia and during active whisking in the awake state (O'Connor et al., 2002; Ros et al., 2009; Popa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Sensory-evoked responses are observed in Crus I following whisker stimulation.
source: Sensory-evoked responses are observed in Crus I following whisker stimulation (Shambes et al., 1978; Bower et al., 1981; Chadderton et al., 2004; Bosman et al., 2010), and whisker movements can be evoked by optogenetic activation of this lobule (Proville et al., 2014), but the principles by which cerebellar neurons encode features of whisking remain to be determined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Whisker movements can be evoked by optogenetic activation of Crus I.
source: Sensory-evoked responses are observed in Crus I following whisker stimulation (Shambes et al., 1978; Bower et al., 1981; Chadderton et al., 2004; Bosman et al., 2010), and whisker movements can be evoked by optogenetic activation of this lobule (Proville et al., 2014), but the principles by which cerebellar neurons encode features of whisking remain to be determined.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The principles by which cerebellar neurons encode features of whisking remain to be determined.
source: Sensory-evoked responses are observed in Crus I following whisker stimulation (Shambes et al., 1978; Bower et al., 1981; Chadderton et al., 2004; Bosman et al., 2010), and whisker movements can be evoked by optogenetic activation of this lobule (Proville et al., 2014), but the principles by which cerebellar neurons encode features of whisking remain to be determined.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Purkinje cells are the final stage of information processing and sole output of the cerebellar cortex.
source: In this study, we set out to identify two key aspects of whisking behavior representation in Purkinje cells (PCs), the final stage of information processing and sole output of the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: Whisking is a rhythmic process characterized both by fast oscillatory forward and backward movements, as well as slower positional changes.
source: Whisking is a rhythmic process characterized both by fast oscillatory forward and backward movements, as well as slower positional changes (Hill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Distinct brain regions make different functional contributions to the encoding of whisking behavior.
source: Distinct brain regions make different functional contributions to the encoding of this behavior (Kleinfeld et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Within the neocortex, the phase of whisking is strongly represented in primary somatosensory cortex (vS1).
source: For example, within the neocortex, the phase of whisking is strongly represented in primary somatosensory cortex (vS1, Curtis et al., 2009), whereas slower changes (e.g. the set point and amplitude of whisker movement) are more closely correlated with activity in primary motor cortex (vM1, Carvell et al., 1996; Hill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Slower changes in whisker movement (e.g. the set point and amplitude) are more closely correlated with activity in primary motor cortex (vM1).
source: For example, within the neocortex, the phase of whisking is strongly represented in primary somatosensory cortex (vS1, Curtis et al., 2009), whereas slower changes (e.g. the set point and amplitude of whisker movement) are more closely correlated with activity in primary motor cortex (vM1, Carvell et al., 1996; Hill et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Changes in both the rate and timing of action potential firing may play a role in sensorimotor encoding.
source: Changes in both the rate and timing of action potential firing may play a role in sensorimotor encoding (De Zeeuw et al., 2011), and it has been proposed that the cerebellum may serve a general function as a linear coding device (Fujita, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It has been proposed that the cerebellum may serve a general function as a linear coding device.
source: Changes in both the rate and timing of action potential firing may play a role in sensorimotor encoding (De Zeeuw et al., 2011), and it has been proposed that the cerebellum may serve a general function as a linear coding device (Fujita, 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: These concepts have not been directly confirmed in the intact brain.
source: However, these concepts have not been directly confirmed in the intact brain, and thus the cerebellar coding scheme(s) employed in the representation of whisker movement is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The cerebellar coding scheme(s) employed in the representation of whisker movement is unknown.
source: However, these concepts have not been directly confirmed in the intact brain, and thus the cerebellar coding scheme(s) employed in the representation of whisker movement is unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Purkinje cells integrate hundreds of thousands of discrete synaptic inputs.
source: PCs integrate hundreds of thousands of discrete synaptic inputs (Palkovits et al., 1977) across a complex non-linear dendritic tree (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980a, 1980b; Finch and Augustine, 1998; Roth and Häusser, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Purkinje cells have a complex non-linear dendritic tree.
source: PCs integrate hundreds of thousands of discrete synaptic inputs (Palkovits et al., 1977) across a complex non-linear dendritic tree (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980a, 1980b; Finch and Augustine, 1998; Roth and Häusser, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Single Purkinje cells accurately encode ongoing whisker movements via bidirectional modulation of simple spike firing rate in a linear manner.
source: Despite this complexity, our experiments demonstrate that single PCs accurately encode ongoing whisker movements via bidirectional modulation of simple spike firing rate in a linear manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from patch clamp recordings.

claim: The results establish the presence of a whisking coordinate system in the cerebellum.
source: Our results establish the presence of a whisking coordinate system in the cerebellum and reveal the computational algorithm employed during sensorimotor processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the linear encoding of whisker position by Purkinje cells.

claim: The results reveal the computational algorithm employed during sensorimotor processing.
source: Our results establish the presence of a whisking coordinate system in the cerebellum and reveal the computational algorithm employed during sensorimotor processing.
evidence: This is inferred from the linear relationship between firing rate and whisker position.

claim: Mice spent variable amounts of time engaged in free whisking, spontaneously switching between periods of whisking and non-whisking behavior.
source: Mice spent variable amounts of time engaged in free whisking, spontaneously switching between periods of whisking and non-whisking behavior (mean whisking bout: 1.68 ± 0.04 s, range: 0.50 – 29.71 s; mean quiet period: 7.82 ± 0.25 s, range: 0.5 – 153.1 s).
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations during recordings.

claim: Mean whisking bout duration was 1.68 ± 0.04 s, with a range of 0.50 – 29.71 s.
source: Mice spent variable amounts of time engaged in free whisking, spontaneously switching between periods of whisking and non-whisking behavior (mean whisking bout: 1.68 ± 0.04 s, range: 0.50 – 29.71 s; mean quiet period: 7.82 ± 0.25 s, range: 0.5 – 153.1 s).
evidence: This is based on measurements from behavioral recordings.

claim: Mean quiet period duration was 7.82 ± 0.25 s, with a range of 0.5 – 153.1 s.
source: Mice spent variable amounts of time engaged in free whisking, spontaneously switching between periods of whisking and non-whisking behavior (mean whisking bout: 1.68 ± 0.04 s, range: 0.50 – 29.71 s; mean quiet period: 7.82 ± 0.25 s, range: 0.5 – 153.1 s).
evidence: This is based on measurements from behavioral recordings.

claim: 70 Purkinje cells were recorded from 47 mice.
source: PCs (n = 70 from 47 mice) could be identified via classification of their two distinct spike waveforms - simple spikes (SS) and complex spikes (CS) - evident in both cell-attached and whole cell recordings (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental dataset.

claim: Purkinje cells can be identified via classification of their two distinct spike waveforms - simple spikes (SS) and complex spikes (CS).
source: PCs (n = 70 from 47 mice) could be identified via classification of their two distinct spike waveforms - simple spikes (SS) and complex spikes (CS) - evident in both cell-attached and whole cell recordings (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Purkinje cell electrophysiology.

claim: Simple spikes and complex spikes are evident in both cell-attached and whole cell recordings.
source: PCs (n = 70 from 47 mice) could be identified via classification of their two distinct spike waveforms - simple spikes (SS) and complex spikes (CS) - evident in both cell-attached and whole cell recordings (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is demonstrated in the experimental recordings shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Tactile whisker stimulation can change the rate of both simple spikes and complex spikes.
source: Although tactile whisker stimulation can change the rate of both SS and CS (Bower and Woolston, 1983; Loewenstein et al., 2005; Bosman et al., 2010), it is not known whether free whisking also affects PC activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It is not known whether free whisking affects Purkinje cell activity.
source: Although tactile whisker stimulation can change the rate of both SS and CS (Bower and Woolston, 1983; Loewenstein et al., 2005; Bosman et al., 2010), it is not known whether free whisking also affects PC activity.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: In the absence of movement, Purkinje cells fired simple spikes at high frequencies (61.9 ± 3.7 Hz, range: 20.1 – 187.9 Hz, n = 70).
source: In the absence of movement, PCs fired SSs at high frequencies (61.9 ± 3.7 Hz, range: 20.1 – 187.9 Hz, n = 70), while the basal rate of CSs was low (1.6 ± 0.1 Hz, range: 0.5 – 3.3 Hz, n = 70).
evidence: This is based on measurements from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The basal rate of complex spikes was low (1.6 ± 0.1 Hz, range: 0.5 – 3.3 Hz, n = 70).
source: In the absence of movement, PCs fired SSs at high frequencies (61.9 ± 3.7 Hz, range: 20.1 – 187.9 Hz, n = 70), while the basal rate of CSs was low (1.6 ± 0.1 Hz, range: 0.5 – 3.3 Hz, n = 70).
evidence: This is based on measurements from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: These firing rate values are consistent with other recordings made from lateral cerebellar Purkinje cells in awake animals.
source: These values are consistent with other recordings made from lateral cerebellar PCs in awake animals (Fu et al., 1997a, 1997b; Lang et al., 1999; Bosman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During bouts of free whisking, a large proportion of Purkinje cells (47 out of 70 cells, ~67%) exhibited significant changes in simple spike rate.
source: During bouts of free whisking, a large proportion of PCs (47 out of 70 cells, ~67%) exhibited significant changes in SS rate (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The majority of Purkinje cells (40/47) increased their firing rates during whisking.
source: While the majority of PCs (40/47) increased their firing rates (Figure 1D, Video 1), in some PCs (7/47) SS rates decreased during whisking (Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological recordings, with examples shown in figures and videos.

claim: In some Purkinje cells (7/47) simple spike rates decreased during whisking.
source: While the majority of PCs (40/47) increased their firing rates (Figure 1D, Video 1), in some PCs (7/47) SS rates decreased during whisking (Figure 1E, Video 2).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological recordings, with examples shown in figures and videos.

claim: Whisker movement was associated with an overall enhancement of the activity of Purkinje cells.
source: Whisker movement was associated with an overall enhancement of the activity of PCs (Figure 1F, G), although the direction and amplitude of SS rate change during whisking was not related to baseline SS firing rates (r = 0.06, p=0.69, n = 47).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1F, G.

claim: The direction and amplitude of simple spike rate change during whisking was not related to baseline simple spike firing rates.
source: Whisker movement was associated with an overall enhancement of the activity of PCs (Figure 1F, G), although the direction and amplitude of SS rate change during whisking was not related to baseline SS firing rates (r = 0.06, p=0.69, n = 47).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the data.

claim: Simple spike rate changes were non-uniform in both magnitude and sign across the population.
source: SS rate changes were therefore non-uniform in both magnitude and sign across the population, with individual PCs exhibiting changes ranging from +128% to -34% during whisking periods (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Individual Purkinje cells exhibited simple spike rate changes ranging from +128% to -34% during whisking periods.
source: SS rate changes were therefore non-uniform in both magnitude and sign across the population, with individual PCs exhibiting changes ranging from +128% to -34% during whisking periods (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is based on measurements from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of simple spike firing was close to 1 both when mice were at rest (0.9 ± 0.1, range: 0.3 – 6.2, n = 70) and when they actively moved their whiskers (0.8 ± 0.1, range: 0.3 – 2.5, n = 70).
source: Overall, the CV was close to 1 both when mice were at rest (0.9 ± 0.1, range: 0.3 – 6.2, n = 70), and when they actively moved their whiskers (0.8 ± 0.1, range: 0.3 – 2.5, n = 70).
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike timing variability from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Significant changes in simple spike variability occurred during free whisking in the majority of Purkinje cells that displayed rate modulation (44/47 PCs).
source: Significant changes in SS variability occurred during free whisking in the majority of PCs that displayed rate modulation (44/47 PCs; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of spike timing variability.

claim: Nearly one third (n = 20/70) of Purkinje cells demonstrated changes in simple spike firing regularity alone.
source: Moreover, nearly one third (n = 20/70) of PCs demonstrated changes in SS firing regularity alone, suggesting that the temporal patterning of SS might independently encode whisker-related signals.
evidence: This is based on analysis of spike timing variability from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The temporal patterning of simple spikes might independently encode whisker-related signals.
source: Moreover, nearly one third (n = 20/70) of PCs demonstrated changes in SS firing regularity alone, suggesting that the temporal patterning of SS might independently encode whisker-related signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some cells show changes in timing without rate changes.

claim: Simple spike activity – either rate, CV, or both - was altered in nearly all Purkinje cells (67/70).
source: In summary, SS activity – either rate, CV, or both - was altered in nearly all PCs (67/70).
evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Locomotion can alter whisking behavior: whisker protraction is correlated with running speed.
source: Locomotion can alter whisking behavior: whisker protraction is correlated with running speed (Sofroniew et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: During the course of Purkinje cell recordings, mice rarely ran on the treadmill (fraction of all whisking bouts spent running was 3.5%).
source: During the course of our PC recordings, mice rarely ran on the treadmill (fraction of all whisking bouts spent running was 3.5%; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on behavioral observations during recordings.

claim: In recordings that included periods of locomotion (n = 10), whisker movements were more protracted.
source: However, in recordings that included periods of locomotion (n = 10), whisker movements were more protracted (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C) and SS firing rates were elevated, independent of the sign of whisking-related modulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; p=0.03, paired t test).
evidence: This is based on analysis of whisker position during locomotion.

claim: Simple spike firing rates were elevated during locomotion, independent of the sign of whisking-related modulation.
source: However, in recordings that included periods of locomotion (n = 10), whisker movements were more protracted (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, C) and SS firing rates were elevated, independent of the sign of whisking-related modulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D; p=0.03, paired t test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of firing rates during locomotion.

claim: Running may influence both whisking behavior and whisker-driven simple spike activity in the cerebellum.
source: These results indicate that running may influence both whisking behavior and whisker-driven SS activity in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in whisker position and firing rates during locomotion.

claim: Significant differences in complex spike firing rates were observed between whisking and non-whisking conditions in a large proportion of Purkinje cells (33 out of 70 cells).
source: Significant differences in CS firing rates were also observed between whisking and non-whisking conditions in a large proportion of PCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; 33 out of 70 cells, p<0.05, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of complex spike rates.

claim: A common phenomenon in many regions of the cerebellar cortex is an inverse relationship between simple spike and complex spike rate changes during behavior.
source: A common phenomenon in many regions of the cerebellar cortex is an inverse relationship between SS and CS rate changes during behavior (Graf et al., 1988; De Zeeuw et al., 1995; Barmack and Yakhnitsa, 2003; Badura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: There was no consistent relationship between whisker-related changes in complex spike and simple spike frequency.
source: However, there was no consistent relationship between whisker-related changes in CS and SS frequency (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B; r = 0.13, p=0.57).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of the data.

claim: Whisker movements are associated with pronounced alterations in Purkinje cell activity.
source: Overall, whisker movements are associated with pronounced alterations in PC activity, indicating that external drive to Crus I changes activity within cerebellar circuits during bouts of whisking.
evidence: This is based on the observed changes in firing rates during whisking.

claim: External drive to Crus I changes activity within cerebellar circuits during bouts of whisking.
source: Overall, whisker movements are associated with pronounced alterations in PC activity, indicating that external drive to Crus I changes activity within cerebellar circuits during bouts of whisking.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed changes in Purkinje cell activity during whisking.

claim: The changes in Purkinje cell simple spike firing rate during whisking bouts closely mimicked whisker movement.
source: Remarkably, the changes in PC SS firing rate during whisking bouts closely mimicked whisker movement (compare upper and lower panels in Figure 2A), irrespective of the direction of the rate change (Figure 2B, C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the peri-event time histograms shown in Figure 2.

claim: Beyond an overall change in complex spike rate, there was no correspondence between the amplitude/duration of whisker movement and the incidence of complex spikes.
source: Beyond an overall change in CS rate, there was no correspondence between the amplitude/duration of whisker movement and the incidence of CSs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of correlation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Increases and decreases in simple spike, but not complex spike, rate are intimately related to changes in whisker position.
source: Therefore, increases and decreases in SS, but not CS, rate are intimately related to changes in whisker position.
evidence: This is inferred from the close correspondence between simple spike rates and whisker position, but not complex spikes.

claim: Crus I receives both motor and sensory whisker-related inputs.
source: Because Crus I receives both motor and sensory whisker-related inputs (Shambes, et al., 1978; Bower et al., 1981; Proville et al., 2014; ), SS firing rate changes could reflect either efferent motor command, or re-afferent sensory input.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Simple spike firing rate changes could reflect either efferent motor command, or re-afferent sensory input.
source: Because Crus I receives both motor and sensory whisker-related inputs (Shambes, et al., 1978; Bower et al., 1981; Proville et al., 2014; ), SS firing rate changes could reflect either efferent motor command, or re-afferent sensory input.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the known inputs to Crus I.

claim: Two-thirds of Purkinje cells (31/47) exhibited simple spike firing rate changes that preceded whisking onset by a mean of -34.6 ± 7.9 ms.
source: Two-thirds of PCs (31/47) exhibited SS firing rate changes that preceded whisking onset by a mean of -34.6 ± 7.9 ms (Figure 2E), and no clear relationship was observed between the latency and magnitude of whisking related alterations in SS rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on cross-correlation analysis of firing rates and whisker position.

claim: No clear relationship was observed between the latency and magnitude of whisking related alterations in simple spike rate.
source: Two-thirds of PCs (31/47) exhibited SS firing rate changes that preceded whisking onset by a mean of -34.6 ± 7.9 ms (Figure 2E), and no clear relationship was observed between the latency and magnitude of whisking related alterations in SS rate (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Temporal relationships between simple spike discharge and whisker movement were preserved when the cross-correlation was calculated based on whisking offset.
source: Temporal relationships were preserved when the cross-correlation was calculated based on whisking offset (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: On average, Purkinje cell simple spike discharge led whisker movement by ~18 ms at the population level.
source: On average, PC SS discharge led whisker movement by ~18 ms (n = 47) at the population level, implying that SS alterations in Crus I predominantly reflect efferent rather than re-afferent signals.
evidence: This is based on cross-correlation analysis of the population data.

claim: Simple spike alterations in Crus I predominantly reflect efferent rather than re-afferent signals.
source: On average, PC SS discharge led whisker movement by ~18 ms (n = 47) at the population level, implying that SS alterations in Crus I predominantly reflect efferent rather than re-afferent signals.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal lead of neural activity relative to movement.

claim: The distribution of temporal correlations was broad (range: -178 ms to 324 ms), and non-unimodal.
source: However, the distribution of temporal correlations was broad (range: -178 ms to 324 ms), and non-unimodal (Figure 2E, Hartigan's dip test; p<0.001, n = 38), indicating that whisking behavior is represented on multiple timescales amongst neighboring PCs within Crus I.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the latency distribution.

claim: Whisking behavior is represented on multiple timescales amongst neighboring Purkinje cells within Crus I.
source: However, the distribution of temporal correlations was broad (range: -178 ms to 324 ms), and non-unimodal (Figure 2E, Hartigan's dip test; p<0.001, n = 38), indicating that whisking behavior is represented on multiple timescales amongst neighboring PCs within Crus I.
evidence: This is inferred from the broad and non-unimodal distribution of latencies.

claim: Delayed Purkinje cell responses relative to whisking may result from additional processing of sensory-driven information and/or recurrent motor-related signals during free whisking.
source: Delayed PC responses relative to whisking may result from additional processing of sensory-driven information and/or recurrent motor-related signals during free whisking.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed delayed responses.

claim: The transmission of whisker signals via parallel fibers of distant granule cells may account for long latency Purkinje cell responses within the cerebellar cortex.
source: In addition, the transmission of whisker signals via parallel fibers (Wilms and Häusser, 2015) of distant granule cells may account for long latency PC responses within the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by citation to previous research on parallel fiber transmission.

claim: Linear regression analysis indicated significant correlations between whisker position and simple spike frequency in over 60% of the Purkinje cells (R2 = 0.958 ± 0.005, p<0.05, ANOVA, n = 44).
source: Plotting whisker position as a function of SS frequency revealed strong linear correlations: linear regression analysis indicated significant correlations in over 60% of the PCs (R2 = 0.958 ± 0.005, p<0.05, ANOVA, n = 44 ).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the relationship between firing rate and whisker position.

claim: Unidirectional Purkinje cells displayed linear changes in simple spike frequency within a range of positions corresponding to only forward or backward movements relative to the whisker resting point.
source: Unidirectional PCs (Figure 3A) displayed linear changes in SS frequency within a range of positions corresponding to only forward or backward movements relative to the whisker resting point (defined as whisker angle during non-movement; see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between firing rate and whisker position shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Unidirectional Purkinje cells were the most common type of response (37/44).
source: These were the most common type of response (37/44) and were associated with either increases or decreases in SS rate.
evidence: This is based on classification of the recorded cells.

claim: In bidirectional Purkinje cells, simple spike frequency both increased and decreased across the full range of movement.
source: In bidirectional PCs, SS frequency both increased and decreased across the full range of movement (Figure 3B), with SS frequency encoding both protracted and retracted whisker positions (7/44 PCs).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the relationship between firing rate and whisker position shown in Figure 3B.

claim: 7 out of 44 Purkinje cells were bidirectional.
source: In bidirectional PCs, SS frequency both increased and decreased across the full range of movement (Figure 3B), with SS frequency encoding both protracted and retracted whisker positions (7/44 PCs).
evidence: This is based on classification of the recorded cells.

claim: Both classes of Purkinje cell displayed almost perfect linear relationships between relative simple spike firing rate change and whisker position (unidirectional: R2 = 0.950 ± 0.004; bidirectional: R2 = 0.959 ± 0.005).
source: Notably, both classes of PC displayed almost perfect linear relationships (unidirectional: R2 = 0.950 ± 0.004; bidirectional: R2 = 0.959 ± 0.005) between relative SS firing rate change and whisker position (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on linear regression analysis of normalized data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In unidirectional cells, simple spike frequency at resting point often differed between bouts of movement and non-movement.
source: In unidirectional cells, SS frequency at resting point often differed between bouts of movement and non-movement.
evidence: This is based on observations from the data analysis.

claim: Bidirectional Purkinje cells never exhibited large baseline shifts in firing frequency.
source: Bidirectional PCs never exhibited such large baseline shifts in firing frequency and were capable of continuously representing whisker position through bouts of whisking and non-whisking via alteration of SS frequency.
evidence: This is based on observations from the data analysis.

claim: Bidirectional Purkinje cells were capable of continuously representing whisker position through bouts of whisking and non-whisking via alteration of simple spike frequency.
source: Bidirectional PCs never exhibited such large baseline shifts in firing frequency and were capable of continuously representing whisker position through bouts of whisking and non-whisking via alteration of SS frequency.
evidence: This is inferred from the continuous linear relationship observed in bidirectional cells.

claim: The gain of simple spike firing rate changes with respect to whisker position varied across cells (mean = 15.8 ± 2.1 Hz/degree).
source: While the gain of SS firing rate changes with respect to whisker position (slope of curves in Figure 3A–C) varied across cells (mean = 15.8 ± 2.1 Hz/degree), bidirectional PCs demonstrated significantly higher gain values in comparison to unidirectional PCs (bidirectional: 33.5 ± 4.4 Hz/degree, unidirectional: 12.5 ± 2.0 Hz/degree, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test), indicating that bidirectional PCs are more sensitive to small-amplitude whisker movements (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the slopes of the linear fits.

claim: Bidirectional Purkinje cells demonstrated significantly higher gain values in comparison to unidirectional Purkinje cells (bidirectional: 33.5 ± 4.4 Hz/degree, unidirectional: 12.5 ± 2.0 Hz/degree, p<0.001).
source: While the gain of SS firing rate changes with respect to whisker position (slope of curves in Figure 3A–C) varied across cells (mean = 15.8 ± 2.1 Hz/degree), bidirectional PCs demonstrated significantly higher gain values in comparison to unidirectional PCs (bidirectional: 33.5 ± 4.4 Hz/degree, unidirectional: 12.5 ± 2.0 Hz/degree, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test), indicating that bidirectional PCs are more sensitive to small-amplitude whisker movements (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of gain values between cell types.

claim: Bidirectional Purkinje cells are more sensitive to small-amplitude whisker movements.
source: While the gain of SS firing rate changes with respect to whisker position (slope of curves in Figure 3A–C) varied across cells (mean = 15.8 ± 2.1 Hz/degree), bidirectional PCs demonstrated significantly higher gain values in comparison to unidirectional PCs (bidirectional: 33.5 ± 4.4 Hz/degree, unidirectional: 12.5 ± 2.0 Hz/degree, p<0.001, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test), indicating that bidirectional PCs are more sensitive to small-amplitude whisker movements (Figure 3C, inset).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher gain values of bidirectional cells.

claim: A strong inverse relationship was observed between the linear encoding range and the gain of individual Purkinje cells.
source: A strong inverse relationship was observed between the linear encoding range and the gain of individual PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) indicating that high-gain PCs linearly encode a relatively smaller portion of all possible whisker angles than low-gain PCs.
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: High-gain Purkinje cells linearly encode a relatively smaller portion of all possible whisker angles than low-gain Purkinje cells.
source: A strong inverse relationship was observed between the linear encoding range and the gain of individual PCs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) indicating that high-gain PCs linearly encode a relatively smaller portion of all possible whisker angles than low-gain PCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the inverse relationship between encoding range and gain.

claim: The fraction of time that a whisker spent within a Purkinje cell's linear encoding regime was approximately constant across the population, with no relationship to Purkinje cell gain.
source: However, the fraction of time that a whisker spent within a PC's linear encoding regime was approximately constant across the population, with no relationship to PC gain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Both high- and low-gain Purkinje cells make similar contributions to the linear encoding of whisker position within the cerebellar cortex.
source: This suggests that both high- and low-gain PCs make similar contributions to the linear encoding of whisker position within the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the constant fraction of time spent within encoding range across different gain values.

claim: Individual Purkinje cells in Crus I represent whisker position linearly and within distinct ranges of movement.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that individual PCs in Crus I represent whisker position linearly and within distinct ranges of movement.
evidence: This is based on the linear correlations observed between firing rate and whisker position.

claim: The high resting firing rate of individual Purkinje cells enables bidirectional representation through both increases and decreases in simple spike firing rate.
source: The high resting firing rate of individual PCs enables bidirectional representation through both increases and decreases in SS firing rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that cells can both increase and decrease firing rates from a high baseline.

claim: In the majority of Purkinje cells, whisker-related changes in simple spikes lead, or are coincident with, movement.
source: In the majority of PCs, whisker-related changes in SS lead, or are coincident with, movement (Figure 2D), indicating the dominance of efferent rather than re-afferent drive to the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is based on temporal analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The dominance of efferent rather than re-afferent drive to the cerebellar cortex is indicated by the temporal relationship between simple spike changes and movement.
source: In the majority of PCs, whisker-related changes in SS lead, or are coincident with, movement (Figure 2D), indicating the dominance of efferent rather than re-afferent drive to the cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal lead of neural activity.

claim: The contralateral primary motor cortex is a source of excitatory input to Crus I.
source: We explored whether the contralateral primary motor cortex, a source of excitatory input to Crus I (Proville et al., 2014), could provide an efferent drive during voluntary whisking.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Seven out of 15 Purkinje cells displayed significant simple spike firing rate modulation during vM1 inactivation.
source: Seven out of 15 PCs displayed significant SS firing rate modulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B; p<0.05, Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test) with a mean latency to whisker movement of -24.6 ± 11.9 ms (n = 7).
evidence: This is based on recordings during motor cortex inactivation.

claim: Linear representation of whisker position by simple spike firing rate was preserved irrespective of vM1 inactivation.
source: Linear representation of whisker position by SS firing rate was preserved irrespective of vM1 inactivation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Inactivation of vM1 does not degrade the cerebellar representation of whisking.
source: Thus, inactivation of vM1 does not degrade the cerebellar representation of whisking, and whisker-related input to the cerebellum is derived from other cortical or subcortical processing stations.
evidence: This is based on the preserved linear encoding during vM1 inactivation.

claim: Whisker-related input to the cerebellum is derived from other cortical or subcortical processing stations.
source: Thus, inactivation of vM1 does not degrade the cerebellar representation of whisking, and whisker-related input to the cerebellum is derived from other cortical or subcortical processing stations.
evidence: This is inferred from the preserved cerebellar representation during vM1 inactivation.

claim: Neuronal firing locked to specific phases of the whisking cycle has been observed at multiple processing stations in the brain.
source: Whisking is a rhythmic process and neuronal firing locked to specific phases of the whisking cycle has been observed at multiple processing stations in the brain (Yu et al., 2006; Leiser and Moxon, 2007; Curtis and Kleinfeld, 2009; Crochet et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In almost every Purkinje cell (30/31), no significant phase tuning was observed.
source: In almost every cell (30/31; p>0.05, Kuiper test), no significant phase tuning was observed (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of phase tuning.

claim: One Purkinje cell exhibited strong phase preference (modulation depth of 4.8).
source: However, one PC did exhibit strong phase preference (modulation depth of 4.8) .
evidence: This is based on analysis of phase tuning for individual cells.

claim: In the Purkinje cell with phase preference, a reduction in simple spike rate was observed during whisking and the incidence of spiking preferentially occurred during whisker retraction.
source: In this cell, a reduction in SS rate was observed during whisking and the incidence of spiking preferentially occurred during whisker retraction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The vast majority of Purkinje cells did not encode rhythmic variations in whisker position within individual whisking cycles.
source: Overall, the vast majority of PCs did not encode rhythmic variations in whisker position within individual whisking cycles, suggesting that phase information is represented by a small fraction of PCs.
evidence: This is based on the lack of phase tuning in most cells.

claim: Phase information is represented by a small fraction of Purkinje cells.
source: Overall, the vast majority of PCs did not encode rhythmic variations in whisker position within individual whisking cycles, suggesting that phase information is represented by a small fraction of PCs.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that only 1 out of 31 cells showed phase tuning.

claim: Using spike train information from single Purkinje cells, it was possible to accurately recover the dynamics of whisker movements over many seconds.
source: Using spike train information from single PCs, it was possible to accurately recover the dynamics of whisker movements over many seconds (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5A showing reconstruction of whisker movement.

claim: In most Purkinje cells, the movement reconstruction derived from the transfer function was highly reminiscent of the whisker set point.
source: In most PCs, the movement reconstruction derived from the transfer function was highly reminiscent of another kinematic parameter – the set point, which denotes the slowly varying midpoint between the protracted and retracted angles of a single whisking cycle.
evidence: This is based on comparison of reconstructed signals with set point.

claim: Reconstructions based on Purkinje cell simple spike activity were excellent predictors of actual whisker set points (range of correlation coefficient: 0.23 – 0.89, mean = 0.57 ± 0.05, p<0.001, n = 18).
source: Reconstructions based on PC SS activity were excellent predictors of actual whisker set points (Figure 5B; range of correlation coefficient: 0.23 – 0.89, mean = 0.57 ± 0.05, p<0.001, n = 18).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis between reconstructed and actual set points.

claim: Single Purkinje cells reliably encode whisker set point.
source: Therefore, we conclude that single PCs reliably encode whisker set point, and that bidirectional changes in the frequency of simple spiking afford a linear representation of whisker trajectory during voluntary movement.
evidence: This is based on the accurate reconstruction of set point from single cell activity.

claim: Bidirectional changes in the frequency of simple spiking afford a linear representation of whisker trajectory during voluntary movement.
source: Therefore, we conclude that single PCs reliably encode whisker set point, and that bidirectional changes in the frequency of simple spiking afford a linear representation of whisker trajectory during voluntary movement.
evidence: This is based on the linear relationship between firing rate and whisker position.

claim: The cerebellum is an established important brain structure for sensorimotor control.
source: However, very little is known about the role of the cerebellum in whisking, despite the established importance of this brain structure for sensorimotor control (Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Simple spike firing rates change during active whisker movement.
source: We have recorded PC activity in behaving mice and, for the first time, have shown that SS firing rates change during active whisker movement.
evidence: This is based on the experimental recordings presented in the study.

claim: Single Purkinje cells estimate slow changes in whisker position in real time via linear alterations in simple spike frequency.
source: Single PCs estimate slow changes in whisker position in real time via linear alterations in SS frequency to provide accurate information about movement trajectories to downstream neurons.
evidence: This is based on the linear encoding and reconstruction results.

claim: Single Purkinje cells provide accurate information about movement trajectories to downstream neurons.
source: Single PCs estimate slow changes in whisker position in real time via linear alterations in SS frequency to provide accurate information about movement trajectories to downstream neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the accurate encoding of whisker position by Purkinje cells.

claim: The computational algorithm by which the cerebellar cortex encodes sensorimotor input has been widely debated.
source: The computational algorithm by which the cerebellar cortex encodes sensorimotor input has been widely debated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field.

claim: Changes in rate and pauses in firing have been proposed as mechanisms of sensorimotor encoding.
source: Changes in rate (Walter and Khodakhah, 2009) and pauses in firing (De Schutter and Steuber, 2009) have been proposed as mechanisms of sensorimotor encoding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The recordings in behaving animals provide direct support for the proposal that the cerebellar cortex is optimized to perform as a linear coding device.
source: While indirect evidence has been found for both schemes, our recordings in behaving animals provide direct support for the proposal that the cerebellar cortex is optimized to perform as a linear coding device (Fujita, 1982; Walter and Khodakhah, 2006, 2009).
evidence: This is based on the observed linear relationship between firing rate and whisker position, supported by citations.

claim: The strong linearity of Purkinje cell simple spike output is surprising given the range of non-linear ionic conductances present across the Purkinje cell dendritic tree.
source: The strong linearity of PC SS output is surprising given the range of non-linear ionic conductances present across the PC dendritic tree (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980a, 1980b) and suggests that non-linear dendritic conductances might compensate for non-linear synaptic integration within passive PC dendrites (Roth and Häusser, 2001), or alternatively are disengaged during free whisking.
evidence: This is a statement combining the observed linearity with known dendritic properties, supported by citations.

claim: Non-linear dendritic conductances might compensate for non-linear synaptic integration within passive Purkinje cell dendrites.
source: The strong linearity of PC SS output is surprising given the range of non-linear ionic conductances present across the PC dendritic tree (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980a, 1980b) and suggests that non-linear dendritic conductances might compensate for non-linear synaptic integration within passive PC dendrites (Roth and Häusser, 2001), or alternatively are disengaged during free whisking.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed linearity, supported by citation.

claim: Non-linear dendritic conductances might be disengaged during free whisking.
source: The strong linearity of PC SS output is surprising given the range of non-linear ionic conductances present across the PC dendritic tree (Llinás and Sugimori, 1980a, 1980b) and suggests that non-linear dendritic conductances might compensate for non-linear synaptic integration within passive PC dendrites (Roth and Häusser, 2001), or alternatively are disengaged during free whisking.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed linearity.

claim: For cerebellar circuits, linear computation may provide the optimal means of performing pattern separation.
source: For cerebellar circuits, linear computation may provide the optimal means of performing pattern separation (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969; Walter and Khodakhah, 2009), affording graded sensorimotor representations (Heiney et al., 2014) that are less prone to saturation, and increasing the dynamic range of the system.
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: Linear computation affords graded sensorimotor representations that are less prone to saturation, and increases the dynamic range of the system.
source: For cerebellar circuits, linear computation may provide the optimal means of performing pattern separation (Albus, 1971; Marr, 1969; Walter and Khodakhah, 2009), affording graded sensorimotor representations (Heiney et al., 2014) that are less prone to saturation, and increasing the dynamic range of the system.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional advantages of linear computation, supported by citation.

claim: Both increases and decreases in firing rate are linear with respect to whisker position, suggesting that molecular layer inhibition plays a crucial role in maximizing the range of cerebellar operation.
source: Both increases and decreases in firing rate are linear with respect to whisker position, suggesting that molecular layer inhibition plays a crucial role in maximizing the range of cerebellar operation (Park et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the bidirectional linear encoding, supported by citation.

claim: The majority of Purkinje cells in Crus I represent changes in whisker set point via simple spike rate changes.
source: The majority of PCs in Crus I represent changes in a simple parameter of whisking behavior, the set point, via SS rate changes.
evidence: This is based on the observed encoding of set point by Purkinje cells.

claim: Because of the close and robust correspondence between simple spike rates and movements, whisker trajectories could be reconstructed with high accuracy using spike trains from individual cells.
source: Because of the close and robust correspondence between SS rates and movements, we were able to reconstruct whisker trajectories with high accuracy using spike trains from individual cells (Figure 5).
evidence: This is based on the reconstruction analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Several Purkinje cells converge onto single target neurons in the deep cerebellar nucleus.
source: Several PCs converge onto single target neurons (Palkovits et al., 1977) in the deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN), ensuring that set point information is propagated downstream, where integration of PC signals (Person and Raman, 2012a) with different rate functions (Figure 3) could further extend the dynamic range of DCN neurons to movement.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Set point information is propagated downstream to the deep cerebellar nucleus.
source: Several PCs converge onto single target neurons (Palkovits et al., 1977) in the deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN), ensuring that set point information is propagated downstream, where integration of PC signals (Person and Raman, 2012a) with different rate functions (Figure 3) could further extend the dynamic range of DCN neurons to movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the convergence of Purkinje cells onto DCN neurons.

claim: Integration of Purkinje cell signals with different rate functions could further extend the dynamic range of deep cerebellar nucleus neurons to movement.
source: Several PCs converge onto single target neurons (Palkovits et al., 1977) in the deep cerebellar nucleus (DCN), ensuring that set point information is propagated downstream, where integration of PC signals (Person and Raman, 2012a) with different rate functions (Figure 3) could further extend the dynamic range of DCN neurons to movement.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional consequences of convergence, supported by citations.

claim: Convergence of positively and negatively modulated Purkinje cell postsynaptic potentials could degrade set point representation.
source: In this arrangement, convergence of positively and negatively modulated PC postsynaptic potentials could degrade set point representation, and therefore it seems likely that these two classes of PC have distinct cellular targets in the DCN (Person and Raman, 2012b).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about circuit organization.

claim: It seems likely that positively and negatively modulated Purkinje cells have distinct cellular targets in the deep cerebellar nucleus.
source: In this arrangement, convergence of positively and negatively modulated PC postsynaptic potentials could degrade set point representation, and therefore it seems likely that these two classes of PC have distinct cellular targets in the DCN (Person and Raman, 2012b).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation.

claim: In contrast to set point, phase information is only sparsely encoded in the cerebellar cortex.
source: In contrast to set point, phase information is only sparsely encoded in the cerebellar cortex (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the lack of phase tuning in most cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: Phase information may be reconstituted in the deep cerebellar nucleus via spatiotemporal convergence of weakly tuned Purkinje cells.
source: However, phase information may be reconstituted in the DCN via spatiotemporal convergence of weakly tuned PCs (De Zeeuw et al., 2011; Person and Raman, 2012b).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Whisker set point is represented by simple spike frequency in the majority of Crus I Purkinje cells.
source: Overall, our data indicate that whisker set point is represented by SS frequency in the majority of Crus I PCs and further suggest that additional phase tuning may restrict SS firing to precise times within the whisking cycle.
evidence: This is based on the observed encoding of set point by Purkinje cells.

claim: Additional phase tuning may restrict simple spike firing to precise times within the whisking cycle.
source: Overall, our data indicate that whisker set point is represented by SS frequency in the majority of Crus I PCs and further suggest that additional phase tuning may restrict SS firing to precise times within the whisking cycle.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the observation of sparse phase tuning.

claim: It is unclear whether the signals recorded correspond to single or multiple whisker movements.
source: It is unclear whether the signals we recorded correspond to single or multiple whisker movements.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation of the study.

claim: Tactile receptive fields of Crus I Purkinje cells can encompass multiple whiskers.
source: Tactile receptive fields of Crus I PCs can encompass multiple whiskers (Bosman et al., 2010), and a similar mapping of motor responses will be helpful to establish how these signals are integrated across the entire cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: A similar mapping of motor responses will be helpful to establish how signals are integrated across the entire cerebellar cortex.
source: Tactile receptive fields of Crus I PCs can encompass multiple whiskers (Bosman et al., 2010), and a similar mapping of motor responses will be helpful to establish how these signals are integrated across the entire cerebellar cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Neurons in the cerebellar cortex potentially have access to discrete 'motor' and 'sensory' representations of whisking behavior.
source: Neurons in the cerebellar cortex potentially have access to discrete 'motor' and 'sensory' representations of whisking behavior: specifically, efferent copy of planned or current movement from cortical and sub-cortical centers, and re-afferent signals providing continuous sensory feedback from the trigeminal nuclei and sensory neocortex about the consequences of voluntary movement .
evidence: This is based on knowledge of cerebellar inputs.

claim: Sensory re-afferent signals are delayed with respect to movement as they are required to propagate from the periphery.
source: Necessarily, sensory re-afferent signals are delayed with respect to movement (Bower et al., 1981) as they are required to propagate from the periphery, and whisker movements are themselves delayed with respect to muscle activity (by a few tens of milliseconds) owing to inertia (Berg and Kleinfeld, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Whisker movements are delayed with respect to muscle activity (by a few tens of milliseconds) owing to inertia.
source: Necessarily, sensory re-afferent signals are delayed with respect to movement (Bower et al., 1981) as they are required to propagate from the periphery, and whisker movements are themselves delayed with respect to muscle activity (by a few tens of milliseconds) owing to inertia (Berg and Kleinfeld, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The majority of Purkinje cells exhibited changes in simple spike activity that preceded or were coincident with movement, consistent with a feed-forward as opposed to feedback representation of whisking in the cerebellum.
source: In our recordings, the majority of PCs exhibited changes in SS activity that preceded or were coincident with movement, consistent with a feed-forward as opposed to feedback representation of whisking in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is based on the temporal analysis of neural activity relative to movement.

claim: The primary motor cortex does not provide the source of efferent drive to the cerebellum during whisking.
source: The primary motor cortex does not provide the source of this efferent drive, as the cerebellar representation remains intact during transient vM1 inactivation.
evidence: This is based on the preserved cerebellar encoding during vM1 inactivation.

claim: Processing stations in the midbrain and the brainstem are likely candidates to provide information to the cerebellum about whisker position during voluntary movement.
source: Processing stations in the midbrain and the brainstem are therefore likely candidates to provide information to the cerebellum about whisker position during voluntary movement.
evidence: This is inferred from the elimination of motor cortex as the source of efferent drive.

claim: The nervous system retains an internal representation of whisking in the cerebellum via a simple linear encoding regime.
source: The nervous system retains an internal representation of whisking in the cerebellum via a simple linear encoding regime.
evidence: This is based on the observed linear encoding of whisker position.

claim: The linear encoding regime grants flexibility to fine-tune and coordinate whisker movement by providing fast online feedback.
source: This grants a remarkable degree of flexibility to fine-tune and coordinate whisker movement by providing fast online feedback, and to disambiguate representations of self- and externally generated sensory signals (Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The linear encoding regime helps disambiguate representations of self- and externally generated sensory signals.
source: This grants a remarkable degree of flexibility to fine-tune and coordinate whisker movement by providing fast online feedback, and to disambiguate representations of self- and externally generated sensory signals (Wolpert et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional significance of the findings, supported by citation.

claim: The resolution with which movement trajectories can be recovered from single neurons suggests that the cerebellar cortex may be an interesting alternative target for brain-machine interface devices.
source: The resolution with which movement trajectories can be recovered from single neurons suggests that the cerebellar cortex may be an interesting alternative target for brain-machine interface devices that seek to restore movement via online decoding of neural signals (Kohler et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, supported by citation.

claim: By providing rapid information about current or future movement, the cerebellar machinery may circumvent long delays in cortical feedback loops, serving effective sensory processing and motor control during active whisking.
source: By providing rapid information about current or future movement, the cerebellar machinery may circumvent long delays in cortical feedback loops, serving effective sensory processing and motor control during active whisking (Rahmati et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the functional role of the cerebellum, supported by citation.

claim: By rendering an internal representation of the whisker system, Purkinje cell spike train dynamics are highly informative about movement trajectories, facilitating active sensation and tactile exploration.
source: Crucially, our findings confirm that by rendering an internal representation of the whisker system, PC spike train dynamics are highly informative about movement trajectories, facilitating active sensation and tactile exploration.
evidence: This is based on the accurate encoding and reconstruction of whisker trajectories.
